sources.cite: Adult critical care nursing certification exam handbook: Behavioral/Psychosocial within Musculoskeletal, Neurological, Behavioral/Psychosocial (18%)
sources.note: Relayed from the course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/ccrn.ts), which read it 2026-10-31; the objective title is the course's own.

sources.cite: Keppra (levetiracetam) prescribing information, revised 8/2023: 5.1 'may cause behavioral abnormalities and psychotic symptoms'; patients 'should be monitored for psychiatric signs and symptoms'; 5.2 antiepileptic drugs 'increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior', so patients should be monitored for 'the emergence or worsening of depression, suicidal thoughts or behavior, and/or any unusual changes in mood or behavior'; 17: report behaviors of concern at once
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the FDA label PDF (summarizing fetch with quotes). The sim names no dose and changes no order: the nurse reports the effect and the prescriber decides.

sources.cite: NIMH, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) Toolkit, information sheet: four questions and a fifth acuity question asked after any yes; a yes to it is an acute positive, 'imminent risk', that needs a STAT safety and full mental health evaluation, and the patient 'cannot leave until evaluated for safety'; a non-acute positive needs a brief suicide safety assessment; refusing to answer counts as positive
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in NIMH's PDF (summarizing fetch with short quotes). The four questions: a wish to be dead, feeling others would be better off, thoughts of suicide in the past week, any attempt ever. 'Clinical judgment can always override a negative screen.' Validated for youth and adult medical patients, including adult medical inpatients (Horowitz et al., Psychosomatics 2020); the toolkit has emergency department, inpatient and outpatient pathways (NIMH adult toolkit page, read the same day). The questions are paraphrased in the sim.

sources.cite: NIMH, Adult ASQ Toolkit: Brief Suicide Safety Assessment guides, nursing scripts and suicide risk screening pathways for the emergency department, the inpatient medical/surgical unit and outpatient primary care and specialty clinics
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch): an index page; the pathways themselves were not opened, so what each setting does after a positive screen is taken from the information sheet.

sources.cite: The Joint Commission, R3 Report Issue 18: National Patient Safety Goal for suicide prevention, NPSG.15.01.01 (effective 2019-07-01): EP1 environmental risk assessment; EP2 screen 'using a validated screening tool'; EP3 an assessment that 'directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors'; EP4 document the risk level and the mitigation plan; EP5-EP7 policies for monitoring, discharge counseling and follow-up
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; issue dated 2019-11-20, updated 2025-12-03). The report names one-to-one monitoring as a key protocol on nonpsychiatric units; it does not itself require it, so the observation level in each sim is the facility's policy.

sources.cite: The Columbia Lighthouse Project, Columbia Protocol (C-SSRS) triage page: 'the most worrisome answers are a recent (past month) yes to items 4 or 5' (intent, intent with a plan) 'and/or any recent (3 months) behavior'; next steps 'are setting specific', and 'interventions should be changed to reflect your individual resources and policies'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; page last modified 2024-03-22). The screener's items, relayed from the NCMHCE session (read 2026-11-11): wish to be dead; suicidal thoughts; thoughts with method; intent without plan; intent with plan; suicidal behavior.

brief.situation: Joanne Pike, 52 (a fictional patient), is on day 6 in the neuro ICU after a subarachnoid hemorrhage; her aneurysm was coiled on day 1. She is awake and oriented, her neuro checks are stable and she has had no seizures. She has been on levetiracetam since admission. Her husband told you this morning, 'This isn't her. She's never been like this.' At 14:00 she has snapped at two staff members, and as you reposition her she says, 'What's the point of any of this? I'd be better off dead.' She has no psychiatric history. You are her critical care nurse, with one other patient; you have about 30 minutes.
handover: SAH day 6, aneurysm coiled; neuro checks stable; no seizures; on levetiracetam since admission.
Husband: 'This isn't her.' Unit policy: a positive suicide screen gets constant observation and a room check until the provider's assessment.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Joanne answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her trust, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say.
Your time ends at 30 minutes. Afterward you write a short risk formulation, then document the risk level and disposition.

source.note: About 30 minutes with one patient in a two-patient ICU assignment (author's scenario timing).

formulation.question: Write your formulation for Joanne: her risk level, what may be causing the change, and what you put in place.

parts.label: Risk level and likely cause
parts.criteria: Names a non-acute positive screen (thoughts in the last few days, none right now, no plan or intent, no attempt) and a new mood change starting after levetiracetam was begun, with no prior history, which the label warns of.
parts.modelAnswer: Non-acute positive: suicidal thoughts in the last few days, none right now, no plan, no intent and no past attempt. The irritability and low mood began a few days after levetiracetam was started, with no history before; the label warns of behavioral changes and suicidal thoughts, so the drug is a likely contributor.

parts.label: What was put in place
parts.criteria: Names constant observation, a room check, the provider called for the safety assessment, the drug raised for review without changing it herself, psychiatry, and her husband told with consent.
parts.modelAnswer: Constant observation and a checked room under the policy; the provider called for the brief suicide safety assessment and psychiatry; levetiracetam raised for review by the provider and pharmacy, with no dose held by me; Mike involved with her consent.

safe.headline: Good: safe, with the drug under review
safe.body: You took the words seriously, screened, kept her safe and connected the timing to a labeled adverse effect without acting on the drug yourself.

unsafe.body: A new mood change with suicidal thoughts on an antiseizure drug labeled for that effect needs a screen, safety and a report, not a note that it is expected.

scoring.modelReasoning: Levetiracetam's label warns of behavioral abnormalities and, like other antiepileptic drugs, of suicidal thoughts. A mood change that starts after the drug, in someone with no history, is reported as a possible adverse effect, and suicidal words are screened at once. The nurse keeps her safe, tells the provider and names the drug; changing or holding it is the prescriber's decision.
